title: World Ocean Temperatures Shatter Records as El Niño Threatens Uncharted Heat
excerpt: Sea surface temperatures hit historic highs in June and July 2026, with scientists warning that a potentially record-breaking El Niño could push the planet into unprecedented warming territory.
body:
• Global sea surface temperatures hit record highs in both June and July 2026, surpassing previous marks from 2023 and 2024
  • July's average sea surface temperature of 20.96°C exceeded the previous July record by 0.07°C, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service
  • A strengthening El Niño — potentially the largest on record — could drive ocean temperatures even higher through early 2027
  • Consequences include coral reef devastation, disrupted fisheries, more intense storms, and reduced ocean capacity to absorb carbon dioxide

Back-to-Back Records

The world's oceans are running a fever that shows no sign of breaking. Global sea surface temperatures shattered records in both June and July 2026, according to data from the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service and Copernicus Marine Service.

On June 21, ocean temperatures reached approximately 21°C, setting an unprecedented mark for that time of year and exceeding previous records from 2023 and 2024 by 0.1°C. July followed with an average sea surface temperature of 20.96°C outside the polar regions — surpassing the previous July record set in 2023 by 0.07°C.

Average sea surface temperatures now hover just hundredths of a degree below the all-time record from March 2024. Given the trajectory of a strengthening El Niño, scientists say surpassing that record is no longer a question of if, but when.

"Current conditions could indicate the beginning of a new phase, leading, once more, to uncharted territory."

— Carlo Buontempo, Director, Copernicus Climate Change Service

El Niño Amplifies the Crisis

Much of the anomalous heat comes from a warm band of water across the tropical Pacific that signals the El Niño climate pattern. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration recently determined that El Niño conditions are officially underway, with the probability of "strong" to "very strong" conditions increasing significantly over the next six months.

Forecasts suggest this El Niño could become the strongest on record. Copernicus seasonal models indicate the event "is likely to reach levels not seen in decades." But El Niño alone doesn't explain what's happening. Wide areas of the northern Pacific and Atlantic, along with much of the Mediterranean Sea, are running significantly hotter than their 1991-2020 average.

"Basically, everywhere on Earth, we're having above-normal temperatures in the ocean," said Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist at Climate Central.

Europe's Seas in Crisis

Europe's seas have been particularly hard hit. The average Mediterranean temperature in July reached 27°C — the highest for any July on record — while an offshore buoy near Mallorca recorded 33°C in early August. An analysis by the World Weather Attribution group found that peak sea temperatures recorded this year in the Mediterranean would have been "virtually impossible" without human-caused climate change.

The heat has contributed to three consecutive months of extreme temperatures across Western and Central Europe, driving widespread drought and record-setting wildfires.

Consequences Cascade

The implications extend far beyond temperature readings. Warmer oceans reduce the capacity to absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, potentially accelerating the pace of global warming. Marine heatwaves threaten fisheries worldwide — El Niño is associated with steep declines in anchovy populations off South America's Pacific coast — and batter coral reef ecosystems already under severe stress.

"It's basically a terrifying time for corals and coral-reef ecosystems," said Amy Apprill, a marine geochemist at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

Hotter seas also increase humidity and overnight temperatures in coastal regions, providing extra energy for storms later in the year. Scientists warn that the coming months could see more records fall as El Niño intensifies.

What's Next

The trajectory gives scientists little reason for optimism. With greenhouse gas emissions continuing to raise the planet's baseline temperature — now approximately 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels — each El Niño cycle pushes the climate system into new territory. The last El Niño event, combined with background warming, drove land and sea temperatures to an all-time high in 2024. This year's event, potentially larger, could surpass even that benchmark. The ocean, which absorbs 93 percent of the additional heat trapped by greenhouse gases, may be approaching a tipping point in its capacity to buffer the atmosphere from the full impact of global warming.
